demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
Patient Vignette: Priya K.

Priya is a 23-year-old South Asian woman, married for two years, who works as a UX designer for a mid-sized tech firm. She presents as meticulously dressed, but there is a tremor in her hands that she tries to hide by clasping them in her lap. She speaks in a low, careful voice, as if afraid of the weight her words might carry.

The accident happened eight months ago, on a rainy Tuesday evening. Priya had just finished a late meeting and was driving home on the freeway. She remembers the exact second—6:47 PM. She glanced down at her phone to change the navigation, just for a moment. When she looked up, a motorcycle was stopped directly in front of her. There was no time to brake. The impact was a sound she says she will never forget: a wet, metallic crunch that she can still hear in silence.

The man on the motorcycle, a 34-year-old father of two, lost his leg below the knee. Priya knows his name, his children’s ages, and the color of the hospital room where she sat for three hours before the doctors told her he would live. She was not charged with a crime—distracted driving warnings, a fine—but she carries a sentence that no court could impose.

In the weeks following, Priya stopped driving. She now takes two buses and a train to get to her office, a commute that adds ninety minutes each way. She tells herself it is environmental, but the truth is more visceral: the moment she sits in a driver’s seat, her chest tightens, her vision narrows, and she feels the phantom sensation of the steering wheel locking under her hands. She has not touched her car keys since the accident.

At work, Priya is a ghost. Her team praises her past work—clean, intuitive interfaces—but she can no longer focus. She stares at wireframes for hours, seeing only the blank spaces where her attention used to be. Her manager has noticed her missed deadlines and the way she startles when a Slack notification pings. She has started taking her lunch breaks in a supply closet because the open-plan office feels too exposed. The fluorescent lights seem too bright, the laughter of colleagues too loud. She feels like everyone is watching her, waiting for her to ruin something else.

At home, her husband, Ravi, tries to help. He cooks dinner, does the laundry, and tells her she is not a bad person. But when he touches her shoulder unexpectedly, she flinches. She has stopped sleeping in their bed. The nightmares come most nights—not the accident itself, but variations: she is on the motorcycle, she is the one bleeding, or she is standing over the man as he asks her why she did not look. She wakes up gasping, her hands clutching the sheets as if they were a steering wheel.

Priya has become hypervigilant in ways that exhaust her. She cannot walk through a parking lot without scanning every car for movement. She flinches at the sound of a car horn. She has stopped crossing streets without waiting for the walk signal three times. Her mother-in-law has commented that she seems "jumpy," and Priya has learned to smile and blame it on caffeine.

Her greatest shame is the avoidance. She has not visited her own parents in six months because they live across town, and the drive makes her nauseous. She deleted all social media because she could not bear to see the man’s family posting updates about his recovery. She stopped going to the gym because the treadmills sound too much like an engine revving.

Priya sits in the therapy room now, her hands still trembling. She looks at the therapist with eyes that hold a question she cannot yet ask: How do I live with what I did? She has not said the word "forgiveness" out loud. She is not sure she deserves to.
